text: This demo is sixteen point nine gigabytes. That's bigger than most finished games I own.
Seven hundred and seventy megabytes of it is a file they forgot to delete. And there are three people on this team.
Expedition: Into Darkness is a medieval extraction crawler. You go down with a torch, you fill your bag, and you try to get back out.
Nine hundred and eleven reviews, sixty nine percent positive. Mixed, in Steam's words. And about a thousand people are in it right now.
The median reviewer had five hours on it. The top ten percent, thirty six. One of them, two hundred and thirteen.
So people are staying. The argument is about everything around the game, not the game.
Steam publishes a file list for every demo, so let's go through what three people actually shipped.
It's Unity, and the code is C# — you can tell because the build has a GameAssembly.dll, which is what the IL2CPP compiler leaves behind.
That's C# translated into C plus plus and compiled native. You write the easy language and ship the fast one.
Audio is FMOD Studio, with Google's Resonance Audio next to it for spatial sound.
In a game where the thing about to kill you is behind you in the dark, that isn't decoration. That's the one middleware I'd argue three people should pay for.
There's also a native plugin in there called RFLib_CNative. It shows up in other Unity games and I could not work out what it does. If you know, the comments are right there.
Now the size, because that's the story here.
One scene in the whole build. Twenty three kilobytes. Everything else streams in from fifteen hundred and fifty five Addressable bundles.
Those bundles are fifteen and a half gigabytes. The single biggest one is two gigabytes on its own.
Some of that is honest. Look at the crafting screen: every weapon is separate parts, a shaft and a head, each with its own durability and inertia.
That means a mesh and a texture set for every part, not every weapon. Armour is the same, piece by piece. Content adds up fast when it's modular.
But three people did not hand-model sixteen gigabytes of medieval kit. My guess is bought libraries and scanned assets, dropped in at source resolution.
And that's usually what a two gigabyte bundle means. Not too much art. Art that never got its compression settings looked at.
Then there's the file that isn't art at all.
GameAssembly.pdb. Seven hundred and forty five megabytes of debug symbols, shipped to players.
Symbols are how you read a crash report. They belong on your build server, not in the download. Nobody has ever needed them to play a game.
With the other four, that's seven hundred and seventy megabytes of a demo doing nothing.
And the store page says you need eight gigabytes of storage. The build is sixteen point nine.
None of this is incompetence. It's what happens when there are three of you and nobody owns the build.
Which shows up in the reviews exactly where you'd expect.
Performance is the loudest complaint by a distance. Blurry, poorly optimised, and a volumetric fog you can't turn off.
Co-op, meanwhile, gets a hundred and six mentions in positive reviews and eight in negative ones. Three people built five player netcode that works.
And people who recommended it had played seven and a half hours. People who didn't, one.
Here's the whole teardown on one card.
Unity, IL2CPP, so the code is C#. Three people. FMOD and Resonance for audio. And seven hundred and seventy megabytes of debug symbols nobody meant to ship.
Worth a dip, and it's free while the early access date moves around.
If you're shipping this year, two checkboxes. Strip your symbols. Then open your own store page and check the number you wrote for storage.
That's my read of it from the outside. If you made this and I got something wrong, say so in the comments and I'll pin the correction.
Next time, another demo, another file list. This is Demo Dip.
